blocks.text: Abstract
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Abstract

blocks.text: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning seeks to decompose a target molecule into commercially available building blocks through a sequence of feasible reactions. The vast combinatorial search space makes this task challenging even for expert chemists. Traditional methods combine tree search with offline-trained value networks that score candidates in isolation, without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task, but relies on simple interfaces that limit exploration of the full search space. We introduce RETROAGENT, an LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning through a harness with structured memory. Through memory and chemistry tools, the agent observes the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, enabling informed decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that RETROAGENTdelivers strong performance and generalization. /githubCode:https://github.com/SXKDZ/RetroAgent

blocks.text: Introduction
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Introduction

blocks.text: Retrosynthetic analysis, the process of identifying synthetic routes to a target molecule from commercially available starting materials, is central to chemical research and drug development (Corey and Wipke, 1969). Modern computational retrosynthesis decomposes this problem into two components (Dong et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2023; Tu et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2024): a single-step retrosynthesis model that predicts candidate reactions for a given molecule, and a multi-step planner that orchestrates the overall search by iteratively calling the predictor. As illustrated in Figure 1(a), given a target molecule, the planner iteratively selects a frontier molecule, queries the single-step model for candidate reactions, expands the search tree, and filters invalid candidates until a valid route is found. The search space grows combinatorially with route depth, making multi-step retrosynthesis an inherently long-horizon planning task: decisions made early constrain downstream options, and a suboptimal choice can lead the search into regions where no feasible route exists. For the single-step component, template-based models (Segler and Waller, 2017) classify over a library of reaction templates, while template-free approaches (Liu et al., 2017; Schwaller et al., 2019; Tetko et al., 2020; Tu and Coley, 2022) generate product-to-reactant mappings directly. For multi-step planning, research has advanced along two main themes: improving the single-step model through self-play on successful trajectories (Kim et al., 2021), and

Our work brings this insight to retrosynthesis: rather than using the LLM as a value estimator within a fixed search algorithm, or as an unstructured sequential planner, we give the LLM direct control over a structured search process through tool calls. Unlike traditional value functions that score molecules in isolation, an LLM agent can condition decisions on the full search context, enabling adaptive, state-dependent planning. Problem Formulation

blocks.text: Given a target molecule m0 and a set of commercially available building blocks B, the goal of multi-step retrosynthesis planning is to find a synthesis route that decomposes m0 into molecules in B through a sequence of valid reactions. Each reaction applies a retrosynthesis template from a template library T to decompose a product molecule into precursors; a single-step retrosynthesis model f proposes ranked candidate templates for any given molecule. A valid route forms a directed acyclic graph from m0 to building blocks, where every non-building-block molecule has at least one valid decomposition and the target is never consumed as a reactant. The solution space of multi-step retrosynthesis can be naturally represented as an AND-OR graph G= (V M ∪ VR, E) : molecule nodes VM have OR semantics, meaning a molecule is solved if any child reaction is solved, and reaction nodes VR have AND semantics, meaning a reaction is solved only if all child molecules are solved. Starting from the target molecule m0 as the root, the search proceeds by iteratively expanding frontier molecules with candidate reactions from the single-step model, adding reaction nodes and edges E connecting molecules to their child reactions and reactions to their child molecules.

heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured

Environment and Tool Interface

blocks.text: We design an environment where the agent drives the search by calling tools that query and modify an AND-OR graph. The environment maintains the graph as a structured memory that persists across the agent’s interaction turns: each node carries a status σ∈ {Open,Solved}, where a molecule starts as Open and becomes Solved once it is identified as a building block or successfully decomposed. The set of Open leaf molecules forms the search frontier. The agent interacts with this memory through two categories of tools. Memory tools advance the search: the agent retrieves candidate reactions for a frontier molecule, selects which and how many to apply to grow the graph, and inspects the updated frontier to decide which molecule to expand next. Chemistry tools provide auxiliary heuristics such as synthetic accessibility and building block availability for prioritizing among candidates. We provide the full tool specifications in Appendix B. 3

blocks.text: The environment automatically handles status propagation, cycle detection, and frontier computation after each tool call, so the agent never needs to reason about graph consistency and can focus entirely on search strategy. Through this interface, the agent learns to adapt its entire search strategy, including which molecule to prioritize, how many reactions to apply, and when to explore alternatives, rather than following the fixed policies of previous approaches (Chen et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2025). With this interface, the search becomes a sequential decision-making problem. The graph is initialized with the target m0 as the soleOpen node. At each turn, the agent can flexibly invoke tools to query candidate decompositions, expand one or more molecules, inspect node details, or call chemistry tools for heuristic guidance. The multi-turn interaction between agent responses and environment observations forms a complete trajectory that we train end-to-end with RL. The search terminates successfully when a complete route is found, or fails when the budget is exhausted.

When the agent chooses to expand a molecule, the environment executes the expansion and status propagation (Algorithm 1): it adds new reactant nodes, checks each against B, marks building block matches asSolved, and propagates status upward, where a reaction node becomes Solved when all children are solved following AND semantics, and a molecule node becomes Solved when any child reaction is solved following OR semantics. Remarks.We highlight several design choices in the tool interface. First, the agent can apply one or multiple candidate reactions in a single call, creating several OR branches at once. Existing search-based methods expand with all available candidates (Chen et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023), while Retro-R1 (Liu et al., 2025) commits to exactly one reaction per molecule. Our multi-expand design allows the agent to balance between these extremes: it can explore multiple promising reactions to hedge against dead ends while skipping clearly unpromising candidates, all within a single tool call. This allows the agent to immediately assess how close each reaction gets to completion without additional tool calls, reducing episode length and providing a direct signal for prioritizing candidates. Third, the environment pre-filters single-step model predictions that would create cycles or duplicate existing reactions. Experimental Setup

blocks.text: Datasets.Following prior work (Chen et al., 2020), we use a building block set of 23,081,633 commercially available molecules from eMolecules. 1 For RL training, we extract 20,626 target molecules from the USPTO-Full reaction database (Chen et al., 2020), filtered to routes with depth greater than 4, with mean depth 5.93. We evaluate on two benchmarks: (1) USPTO-190: 190 challenging target molecules extracted from USPTO-Full (Chen et al., 2020) with reference routes (mean depth 6.0), serving as the standard in-distribution benchmark; (2) ChEMBL-1000: 1,000 drug-like molecules from the ChEMBL database (Liu et al., 2023), an out-of-distribution dataset without reference routes, used to test generalizability. Single-step model.We follow prior work (Chen et al., 2020) and use a template-based MLP as the single-step retrosynthesis model. The model predicts over 381,302 USPTO reaction templates based on Morgan fingerprints, and uses RDChiral (Coley et al., 2019) for template application and verification. We use the pretrained weights from DESP (Yu et al., 2024). We do not adopt the Retro-R1 weight variants V2, V3, and V4 (Liu et al., 2025): V2 and V3 may produce chemically unrealistic reactions (Genheden and Bjerrum, 2022), and V4 weights are not public. We also do not adopt their two-branch policy that reranks reactions based on predicted probabilities, as we aim to test the learned search capabilities of the agent. Metrics.Following Liu et al. (2025), we report two complementary metrics. Pass@1 measures the fraction of targets solved in a single trajectory, directly reflecting the agent’s decision quality without retry. Success rate at budget N measures the fraction of targets solved within N unique single-step model calls, capturing cumulative performance as the search budget increases. While the budget definition is the same for all methods, searchbased methods consume the full budget within a single deterministic run. LLM-based methods typically cannot exhaust the budget in one trajectory due to the difficulty of longcontext modeling; we therefore follow the iterative evaluation protocol (Liu et al., 2025) and conduct multiple independent trajectories per target with shuffled prediction and frontier orderings, where repeated predictions do not count toward the budget. blocks.text: Model and infrastructure.We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025a) as the base model, a 4B-parameter instruction-tuned model with native tool-calling support. We deliberately choose a smaller model without thinking capabilities to demonstrate that the structured memory interface, rather than raw model capacity, drives planning performance. Training uses the slime framework (Zhu et al., 2025) with Megatron (Shoeybi et al., 2019) for distributed training and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) for inference on 8×H200 GPUs. The tool server runs as a separate process pool with 16 instances, decoupled from the training pipeline; this allows the environment to scale independently of GPU resourc es and avoids blocking gradient computation during tool execution. Hyperparameter configuration.We optimize with Adam ( β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98), a constant learning rate of 1×10−6, and weight decay of 0.01. Each batch samples 32 target molecules with G= 8 rollouts each at temperature 1.0, yielding 256 episodes per batch; with TIS reusing each batch for 2 gradient steps, the effective batch size is 128. The GSPO clip ratio is ϵ= 3.5×10−4, the KL coefficient is β= 0.001, and the TIS clip range is [0.5, 2.0]. Behavioral Analysis (RQ4)

blocks.text: Beyond the ablation numbers, we analyze what search strategy the agent actually learns by examining tool usage evolution and search tree structure (Figure 3), which helps further explain the performance gaps in Table 2. Tool usage evolution.Figure 3(a) shows how tool call ratios change during training. The agent has access to 8 tools: 4 memory tools for search and 4 chemistry tools for heuristic guidance. Chemistry tools are actively used at step 0 ( ∼11%) but collapse to near zero by step 10, suggesting that the building block annotations returned by the prediction tool provide sufficient signal for candidate prioritization. The node inspection tool stays below ∼1% throughout training and quickly drops to near zero, indicating the agent extracts sufficient information from other tool responses. Three tools remain dominant throughout: prediction, expansion, and frontier retrieval. Multi-expand usage emerges around step 120 and becomes dominant after step 350, with the agent applying multiple reactions per call in over 70% of expansions, demonstrating that the agent discovers this strategy through reward shaping rather than being explicitly guided. Search tree structure.Figure 3(b)–(f) plot the search tree structure for each configuration, where each point represents one rollout with its maximum tree depth and total molecule nodes expanded. Comparing across configurations reveals three key findings. First, RL training is essential for long-horizon planning. blocks.text: Conclusion
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Conclusion

blocks.text: We presented RETROAGENT, an RL-trained LLM agent for retrosynthesis planning that operates over an AND-OR graph as structured memory. The environment automatically maintains the search state, while the agent makes strategic decisions through tool calls. With a 4B-parameter model, RETROAGENTachieves the highest pass@1 on USPTO-190 and substantially outperforms all baselines on the out-of-distribution ChEMBL-1000, despite using a smaller model and less training data. Ablation studies confirm that multi-expand and reward shaping are key to the agent’s performance, and behavioral analysis reveals that the agent progressively learns to trade depth for breadth through RL. The strong outof-distribution results suggest that the harness enables generalizable planning strategies rather than dataset-specific memorization. We believe the design principle of combining LLM reasoning with structured environment management is broadly applicable to other long-horizon planning tasks beyond retrosynthesis.

blocks.text: B Tool Interface Details
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
B Tool Interface Details

blocks.text: The agent interacts with the environment through 8 tools divided into two categories. All graph-related tools use symbolic identifiers (M# for molecules, R# for reactions, P# for predictions) rather than raw SMILES strings to prevent copying errors. Memory tools.These tools allow the agent to query and modify the AND-OR graph: •predict_templates(molecule_id) : Queries the single-step retrosynthesis model for a given molecule node. Its 50 highest-scoring predictions are shuffled and truncated to at most k= 20 candidates, each assigned an ID (P1, P2, . . . ) and listing its reactants with per-reactant building block annotations (building_block: true/false). Predictions that would create cycles (a reactant is an ancestor of the molecule) or duplicate an existing reaction are automatically filtered out. Within a rollout, subsequent calls for the same molecule reuse the cached candidates with updated filtering at zero additional budget cost. •expand(molecule_id, prediction_id) : Applies one or more predictions to the graph, creating new reaction and molecule nodes. Multiple prediction IDs can be commaseparated (e.g.,"P1,P3,P5") to create several reaction branches in a single call. Returns the expansion results and the parent node status. •get_frontier() : Returns the current set of Open leaf molecules that have not yet been expanded. Also signals when the root molecule has been solved. •inspect_node(node_id) : Returns detailed information about any node in the graph, including its SMILES, status ( Open/Solved), building block status, parent nodes, and
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
B Tool Interface Details

blocks.text: child nodes. Chemistry tools.These tools provide domain-specific heuristics to help the agent prioritize among candidates. Unlike memory tools, chemistry tools take SMILES strings as input rather than node IDs: •get_molecule_info(molecules) : Returns molecular properties including molecular weight, logP , number of atoms, and ring counts for a list of molecules. •search_building_blocks(molecules) : Checks whether given molecules are available in the building block database and returns their availability status. •calculate_synthetic_accessibility(molecules) : Computes the synthetic accessibility (SA) score (Ertl and Schuffenhauer, 2009) for each molecule, ranging from 1 (easy to synthesize) to 10 (difficult). •calculate_scscore(molecules) : Computes the SCScore synthetic complexity (Coley et al., 2018) for each molecule, ranging from 1 (simple) to 5 (complex).

blocks.text: Related Work
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Related Work

blocks.text: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning methods broadly divide into two streams:search-based methods that ground every step in a validated template set, andmodel-basedmethods that leverage learned representations to generate or predict routes directly. Our work falls within the search-based paradigm: we use a template-grounded single-step model for chemical validity, but replace the fixed search algorithm with an RL-trained LLM agent that learns its own search strategy. Search-based (template-grounded) methods.The dominant paradigm combines a trained single-step retrosynthesis model, typically an MLP classifier over reaction templates (Segler 15
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Related Work

blocks.text: and Waller, 2017), with a search algorithm over the resulting AND-OR graph. Retro* (Chen et al., 2020) introduced neural-guided A* search with a learned value function estimating the cost-to-go for each molecule. PDVN (Liu et al., 2023) improved this with dual value networks that separately predict synthesizability and cost. EG-MCTS (Hong et al., 2023) uses experience from past searches to train a value network for Monte Carlo tree search. 3N-MCTS (Segler et al., 2018) combined MCTS with three neural networks for rollout-based evaluation. GNN-Retro (Han et al., 2022) improves molecule cost estimation by using a graph neural network that aggregates information from structurally similar molecules. DESP (Yu et al., 2024) proposed bidirectional search, interleaving top-down retrosynthetic expansion with bottom-up forward synthesis from building blocks, guided by a learned synthetic distance function. Retro-fallback (Tripp et al., 2024) introduced probabilistic route reliability through stochastic OR nodes. Beyond node-level heuristics, several works incorporate domain-specific insights into improve multi-step retrosynthesis planning. Mo et al. (2021) learn pathway-level representations that rank and cluster retrosynthesis routes by their strategic quality, while Roh et al. (2026) reformulate the single-step prediction itself at a higher level of abstraction, separating strategic disconnections from tactical functional group choices to reduce the effective search space. These methods achieve high solve rates
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Related Work

blocks.text: within large iteration budgets (up to 500 single-step model calls) but encodefixedsearch strategies: the heuristic is always a pretrained value function, and the expansion order is determined by the algorithm, not by per-target reasoning. Template-free and generative methods.Beyond template-based classifiers (Chen and Jung, 2021; Coley et al., 2017; Segler and Waller, 2017), template-free methods generate reactants directly. The Molecular Transformer (Schwaller et al., 2019) and augmented NLP models (Tetko et al., 2020) frame retrosynthesis as sequence-to-sequence translation, while RootAligned (Zhong et al., 2022) enforces a one-to-one mapping between product and reactant tokens by aligning them to a shared root atom. BatGPT-Chem (Yang et al., 2025b) trains an LLM on chemical instruction data for single-step prediction. LLM-Syn- Planner (Wang et al., 2025) uses an LLM to mutate retrieved routes into multi-step plans for new targets. These approaches can leverage broad chemical knowledge but typically lack the structural guarantees of template-grounded methods. LLM agents for retrosynthesis.Recent work has explored LLMs asagentic plannersthat interact with chemistry tools through multi-turn conversations. Retro-R1 (Liu et al., 2025) trains a Qwen2.5-7B agent with PPO to select molecules and reactions through aCALL/SELECT interface, achieving state-of-the-art pass@1 success rates. However, Retro-R1 operates in a linear, no-backtracking mode: the agent commits irrevocably to each reaction selection, with
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Related Work

blocks.text: no ability to revisit alternative branches. Its state representation is implicit: the agent must infer the search state from the conversation history. AOT* (Song et al., 2025) combines an LLM with AND-OR tree search, using the LLM to guide node selection within a traditional search framework. In contrast, our agent has full control over the search process and learns its own strategy end-to-end through RL. D Limitations and Discussion Practicality of the generated routes.Our evaluation follows the standard template-based protocol: a route is considered valid if every step applies a verified reaction template and all leaves terminate at purchasable building blocks, and quality is measured by success rate, search budget, and route length. Because all routes pass through the same validated template set and building-block catalog, the routes RETROAGENTproduces are chemically valid by construction, and the comparison to baselines is on equal footing. However, this notion of validity does not capture full synthetic practicality: factors such as reaction yield, regio- and stereoselectivity, reaction conditions, and protecting-group strategy are not modeled, and a shorter or template-valid route is not necessarily the most practical one in the laboratory. These considerations affect all template-based planners equally and depend on information absent from the benchmarks, which provide only target molecules and, for USPTO-190, reference routes. Inference cost relative to traditional search.RETROAGENTrelies on LLM inference at every search step, which is substantially more expensive than the lightweight value-network or policy lookups used by traditional search algorithms such as Retro* and PDVN. A single planning trajectory issues tens of LLM calls and consumes thousands of tokens, whereas a classical planner evaluates its scoring function in milliseconds. This overhead is the price of the explicit, inspectable reasoning that drives our gains, and we regard it as acceptable in the retrosynthesis setting: planning is a one-time, offline computation of seconds to minutes per target, negligible against the days to weeks required to validate a route experimentally. Nonetheless, for latency-sensitive or very high-throughput screening, traditional search remains more economical, and reducing LLM planning cost (e.g., through smaller distilled policies or selective invocation) is a worthwhile direction.

blocks.text: F Evaluation Protocol
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
F Evaluation Protocol

blocks.text: We evaluate using the standalone eval pipeline with the same tool server as training, with greedy decoding (temperature 0). Each rollout runs for up to 120 turns and a 120K token budget, more generous than training (90 turns, 56K tokens) to allow extra exploration. Following the iterative protocol, each experiment issues successive rollouts for a target until a route is found or the search budget is exhausted; we run 10 independent experiments per target and report the mean and standard deviation, with stochasticity coming entirely from shuffled prediction and frontier orderings in the tool server, not from LLM sampling. A rollout terminates when the root molecule is solved, when maximum turns are reached, when no successful expansion occurs for several consecutive turns (no progress), when the frontier is exhausted (dead frontier), when the token budget is exhausted, or when a single turn exceeds the response limit of 8,192 tokens due to repetition. Reaching the maximum route depth of 30 reaction steps blocks only the offending branch and does not by itself end the rollout. 17

blocks.text: G.1 Same-Backbone Comparison with Retro-R1
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
G.1 Same-Backbone Comparison with Retro-R1

blocks.text: To isolate the contribution of our structured-memory interface from the choice of base model, we reproduce the Retro-R1 two-action ( CALL/SELECT) interface on the same Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbone used by RETROAGENT, holding the model and RL training procedure fixed and varying only the interface. We use the released Retro-R1 code, the step-200 checkpoint, and the same iterative evaluation protocol on USPTO- 190, reporting five independent runs. As shown in Table S2, the Retro-R1 interface on the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbone reaches 45.05 ± 0.29% pass@1, 8.21 points below RETROAGENT(53.26%) on the same backbone and even below the original Retro-R1 result of 50.00% on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M. Thus moving the Retro-R1 interface onto our backbone does not by itself improve performance; the gain comes from the interface and learned policy rather than the base model. Together with the zero-shot result of 4.42% pass@1 (Table 2), this shows the interface does not help without RL training, and that the gains are not attributable to the choice of base model.

blocks.text: G.2 Reward Sensitivity
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
G.2 Reward Sensitivity

blocks.text: We study the sensitivity of RETROAGENTto its reward shaping from two perspectives: the relative weighting of the budget penaltyδN and depth penalty δD, and the overall magnitude of both penalties. All configurations are otherwise identical to RETROAGENTand trained from the same base model. Table S3 reports USPTO-190 success rates as mean±std over five runs. On the relative weighting, keeping both penalty terms is best (53.26%), and dropping either one lowers pass@1 only modestly (budget-only 51.16%, depth-only 50.84%), so the two terms are complementary but performance is robust to their balance. On the magnitude, doubling both penalty rates and caps lowers pass@1 to 48.32% but the budget curve converges (N= 200 rises to 75.58%, approaching the full model’s 78.63%). Harsher penalties make the agent more conservative, trading first-attempt success for budget efficiency without removing the underlying ability to solve targets. blocks.text: Failure Case Analysis
heading_path: RETROAGENT: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured
Failure Case Analysis

blocks.text: We categorize every failed target on USPTO-190 and ChEMBL-1000 by the per-episode termination reason logged by the environment (Table S5). The environment records four mutually exclusive termination reasons: •max_turns: the episode reaches the turn limit (120) without solving the root molecule; •no_progress : the agent makes no successful expansion for five consecutive turns and is stopped early; •dead_frontier: every open molecule has been expanded yet none yields a solved route; •token_limit: the episode exhausts the 120K-token budget. Reaching the maximum route depth of 30 reaction steps only blocks the offending branch rather than ending the episode, so such attempts are subsumed withinmax_turns or no_progress. On both benchmarks, budget exhaustion dominates: max_turns and no_progresstogether account for∼96% of failures on USPTO-190 and∼94% on ChEMBL- 1000, whiledead_frontier andtoken_limit together remain under 7%. Failures are therefore concentrated on hard, deep targets that exhaust the search budget rather than on the agent running out of candidates or hitting action-space limits. We also note that failed targets receive a similar number of first-step predictions as solved ones (15.0 vs. 17.9 on USPTO-190; 16.6 vs. 17.0 on ChEMBL-1000); failures thus arise from exhausting the search budget on hard, deep targets, not from a lack of initial candidates.
